title: Where Is God When It Hurts: Suffering and the Goodness of God
subtitle: A five-session study on the problem of evil, the providence of God, and the hope that does not disappoint.
summary:
This study is for the person who has stood at a hospital bed, or a graveside, or in the wreckage of a marriage or a diagnosis, and asked the oldest question there is: if God is good, and God is able, why this? It's for the skeptic who left the faith over a children's cancer ward and was never given an answer worth the name, and for the Christian still inside the faith who keeps being handed platitudes for a real question. It's for the pastor who has run out of things to say at funerals. It won't promise to solve the problem of evil. No honest book ever has, and the ones that pretend to are the ones that wound. It promises something harder. It takes the objection at its full strength, refuses the cheap answers, and walks toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which isn't an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself.

The five sessions move in order. First, the question stated without flinching, the way a thoughtful atheist states it, so that the believer in the room feels it too. Then providence, held without a tidy resolution: a God who permits what he hates and works it toward an end we can't see from inside it. Then Job, where God answers the sufferer not with an explanation but with a whirlwind of questions, and rebukes the friends who had the formula. Then the cross, where the God who permits suffering doesn't stay outside it but enters it and dies inside it. And last, the hope that doesn't explain suffering away but defeats it: the resurrection, and the new creation where God wipes every tear from every face. This study isn't solving a puzzle from a safe distance. It stands in the rubble with you and points at the one light the dark couldn't put out.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Question That Will Not Quiet
sessions.aim: To state the problem of evil at its full strength, in the form its most thoughtful unbelievers give it, before reaching for any answer, so that the room feels the real weight of the objection and no one is handed a comfort that hasn't first looked the horror in the face.
sessions.summary:
Everything else in this study depends on this session telling the truth, so we begin by refusing the cheap answer. The problem of evil is the oldest argument against God and the strongest, and it isn't strong because clever atheists invented it. It rises off the maternity ward and the cancer floor and the mass grave, off the suffering of children who did nothing to deserve it. Dostoevsky gave it its hardest form in The Brothers Karamazov, where Ivan doesn't deny God but says that if the world's final harmony costs the unavenged tears of one tortured child, he respectfully hands back his ticket. Three claims seem to collide: God is all-good, God is all-powerful, and evil is real. The cheap answers quietly drop one of them.

This session doesn't offer an answer. It offers a posture. The God of the Bible never scolds the sufferer for asking. The Psalms ask, Job asks, and Jesus asks from the cross. The question isn't the enemy of faith, and it's allowed to be as large as it actually is.

keyScripture.why: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). The Bible's own prayer book asks where God is in suffering and isn't rebuked for it. Faith doesn't begin by silencing the question. It begins by being allowed to ask it of God himself.

discussion.q: Before any theology, when you've watched suffering that seemed senseless and undeserved, what question did it raise in you? Did you feel allowed to ask it?
discussion.behind: Bring the real question into the open, not the polite one. Most people have carried it and felt they weren't supposed to. You want the question spoken at its true size, and you want it clear from the first minute that asking is allowed. Go first if the room is slow, and don't rush to answer anything yet.

discussion.q: Ivan Karamazov refuses a happy ending bought with the unavenged suffering of even one tortured child. Where do you feel the force of that? Is there a part of you that thinks he's right?
discussion.behind: Let the room feel the strength of the objection rather than defeat it. The point of this session is that it really is strong. Help people admit that it lands, even for believers, because a faith that can't feel the weight of this question hasn't understood it. Resist the urge to resolve it here.

discussion.q: The three claims in tension are that God is all-good, that God is all-powerful, and that evil is real and terrible. Where have you heard someone solve the problem by quietly letting go of one of them?
discussion.behind: Get the room to name the cheap moves. God isn't really able. Evil is an illusion or a lesson. God is powerful but not good in any sense we'd recognize. Each easy answer survives only by giving up something the Bible won't give up, which is why the problem stays hard.

discussion.q: What's the worst thing you've ever been told, or have said, to someone in real grief, the kind of answer that wounded instead of helped? Why do we reach for those answers so quickly?
discussion.behind: Expose the habit of fixing pain with a formula. Everything happens for a reason. God needed another angel. At least. We hand out these answers mostly to relieve our own discomfort with silence, and the sufferer feels them as a second wound. Go gently; some will recognize their own words.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 13. Where is your own faith most pressed by suffering? Have you ever brought that pressure to God instead of carrying it around him?
discussion.behind: Turn to ourselves, the leader included. You're not trying to manufacture doubt, only to let the room admit that this question presses on real faith, and that bringing it to God is itself an act of faith. The skeptic in the room should feel met here, not managed. Go first.

objections.objection: If God is all-powerful he could stop the suffering of innocent children, and if he's all-good he'd want to. He doesn't. So either he can't, and he isn't the God you preach, or he won't, and he isn't good. There's no third option, and every answer I've heard is a way of refusing to admit it.
objections.response: This is the argument at its strongest, and pretending it's weak would be the first dishonesty. So here's what the study will and won't do with it. It won't dissolve the problem by quietly dropping one of the three claims, because the Bible drops none of them. God is good. God is able. Evil is real and hateful, and Scripture never once calls a murdered child a teaching moment. What the study questions is whether those three leave only two options, a God who can't or a God who won't. The rest of the study walks toward a third possibility the argument can't see from where it stands, that a good and able God might permit for a time an evil he hates, for an end that needs the permitting, and that he doesn't leave us alone inside it. That isn't a proof, and it won't be sold as one. It's a claim that the dilemma isn't as airtight as it looks, made without pretending the suffering is smaller than it is.

objections.objection: You're going to give me an intellectual answer to a wound. My grief isn't a debate I lost. Even an airtight argument wouldn't raise the dead, and the fact that you're reaching for argument at all shows you don't understand what suffering is.
objections.response: You're right, and it may be the most important thing said in the whole first session. An argument doesn't heal a grave. If this study ended in a clever proof, it would have failed, because the problem of evil isn't finally a puzzle to be solved but a wound to be entered, and the Bible knows that better than the philosophers do. God's answer to the worst sufferer in Scripture wasn't a syllogism. It was his presence and a flood of questions that explained nothing. And the deepest word the Bible speaks into suffering isn't an argument at all but a cross, God himself inside the pain. The study starts with the intellectual question because truthfulness requires stating it plainly, but it doesn't end there, and it never claims the answer to grief is a better paragraph. The answer the Bible gives is a Person who entered the dark, and you're right to refuse anything less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What suffering, yours or someone you love, has pressed hardest on whether you can believe God is good? Have you ever said that to God in so many words?
sessions.practice: This week, don't try to answer the question. Sit with it instead. Once, take the suffering that presses hardest on your faith, the loss or the diagnosis or the senseless thing, and bring it to God the way the psalmists did, plainly: how long, why, where are you. Don't apologize for it and don't tidy it. Don't end on a forced note of resolution. If you aren't sure God is there, say that too. Write down what it was like to bring the question to God instead of carrying it around him, and whether being allowed to ask changed how heavy it felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we're not going to pretend tonight. Some of us have seen things that don't fit any tidy story, and we were told to hush about them, and we hushed, and the question only went underground and grew. We bring it up tonight, out loud, where you can hear it. If you're good and you're able, why the child, why the cancer, why the silence? We don't have the answer, and we won't manufacture one. But we've noticed that you don't scold the people who ask. Your own book is full of the question. So we ask it, and we trust that asking it to your face is closer to faith than swallowing it ever was. Stay with us as we look at this. Don't let us settle for an answer too small for the wound. Amen.
reflection: What cheap answer am I most tempted to give when someone is suffering, and whose discomfort is it meant to relieve, theirs or mine?
Which of the three claims, God's goodness, God's power, the reality of evil, do I quietly let go of when the problem gets too heavy, and what does that show me?
Have I felt that asking God the hard question was a failure of faith? What would change if I believed, as the Psalms suggest, that asking is an act of faith?
sessions.teaching:
I want to begin this study by doing what most studies on suffering won't do, which is to state the problem plainly before saying a single comforting word. Every comfort that hasn't first looked the horror in the face is a lie, and the people in this room who are suffering can smell that lie from across the table. So here is the question in its oldest form. If God is perfectly good, he must want to end suffering. If God is all-powerful, he must be able to. Suffering hasn't ended, and not just the suffering of villains getting what they earned, but the suffering of children who did nothing, of faithful people who prayed and got silence, of whole peoples ground into the dirt. So, the argument runs, either God isn't good, or he isn't able, or one of those words doesn't mean what we say it means.

This isn't a trick invented by hostile professors. It's the cry that goes up from every cancer ward and battlefield and every nursery where a small casket had to be built, and it's old. Later writers attributed a version of it to Epicurus, three centuries before Christ. It has never been answered to everyone's satisfaction, and I'll tell you now that I'm not going to answer it to yours either. If I could reduce the suffering of the world to a paragraph that made it all make sense, that paragraph would be obscene.

I want to take the objection at full strength, in the form a great novelist gave it. In The Brothers Karamazov (1880), Dostoevsky gives us Ivan, who isn't a fool or a villain. Ivan doesn't argue that God doesn't exist. He says something worse. Even if there is a God, and even if at the end of all things there is a perfect harmony where every wrong is made right, he can't accept it, because the price is too high. The price includes the unavenged tears of tortured children, suffering no future bliss can justify. So he respectfully hands back his ticket. He won't buy a paradise built on that. I'm a Christian, and I'm telling you that Ivan's objection is one of the strongest things ever said against God, and I don't think it's stupid. I came to faith from atheism, and I won't pretend this wall is low. If you're a skeptic who came tonight braced for a sales pitch, I want you to hear that.

So let's be precise about why the problem is so hard, because the cheap answers all work the same way. There are three claims. God is all-good. God is all-powerful. Evil is real and terrible. All three appear to be true, and they appear to collide, and almost every easy answer survives by quietly letting go of one of them. Some say God isn't really able, that he'd help if he could, and they've traded the God of the Bible for a sympathetic weakling. Some say evil isn't really real, that it's an illusion or a lesson or a stage of growth, and they've stood in front of a grieving mother and called her dead child a teaching tool. Some say God is powerful but not good in any sense we'd recognize, and they've made him a tyrant we obey out of fear. The Bible refuses all three moves. It insists God is good all the way, sovereign all the way, and it never softens evil into something acceptable. Scripture weeps at gravesides; it doesn't lecture.

So we're left holding three things that won't fit, and I'm not going to cheat to make them fit. But here's the first thing I want you to take home. It isn't an answer; it's a posture. The God of the Bible doesn't punish the sufferer for asking. Somehow we've picked up the idea that the faithful response to suffering is to swallow the question and perform a calm we don't feel, as if God were fragile and our candor might offend him. Open the book. The Psalms, the prayer book God gave his people, are full of the question. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1). That last line is the one Jesus prayed from the cross. In the deepest agony there has ever been, the Son of God didn't reach for a serene affirmation. He reached for the Bible's own why. And the book of Job, which gets a whole session, is one long protest, a righteous man demanding an audience with God. At the end God is angry, but not at Job. He's angry at the friends who defended him with tidy theology.

So the question isn't the enemy of faith. It's allowed to be exactly as large as the suffering that raised it, and bringing it to God, to his face, is one of faith's truest acts. You don't cry out to a God you're sure isn't there. Ivan hands back his ticket and walks away. A believer sometimes hands back the ticket and stays in the room, still talking to God. We're going to stay in the room. We'll let the question be as big as it is, and over these five weeks we'll walk toward the one answer I know that the dark couldn't put out, which isn't a proof but a God who came down into the dark himself and hasn't left it. Tonight we just name the question. Next week we ask what it could mean that a good and able God permits what he hates.

scriptureStudy.note: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" The prayer book of Israel asks where God is in suffering and isn't rebuked for it. The cry of the afflicted is a form of faith Scripture models, not its failure.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" David's cry, and the verse Jesus prayed from the cross. The sufferer's why was taken up by the Son himself.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?" The prophet brings unanswered injustice to God as a complaint, and God answers him. The protest belongs inside the relationship, not outside it.

"Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" Job, whom God calls blameless, voices raw despair, and the book doesn't condemn him for it. Anguish spoken to God is not the same as cursing God.

"My soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is; so I say, 'My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD.'" Scripture keeps the words of a man who has lost hope, before any turn toward mercy comes.
"Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?" The prophet asks the oldest form of the problem as a direct question to a God he hasn't stopped trusting.
"Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" Abraham presses God on justice, and God receives it. Scripture honors the demand that God be good.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, trace how old and serious the problem is, which guards against treating it as a modern complaint to be swatted away. A sharp early form of the dilemma, a God either unwilling or unable to prevent evil, was attributed to Epicurus by later writers. David Hume restated it in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (published 1779). In the twentieth century philosophers distinguished a logical form, which claims evil is strictly incompatible with a good and all-powerful God, from an evidential form, which claims the amount and apparent pointlessness of suffering make such a God unlikely. Alvin Plantinga's free will defense, set out in God, Freedom, and Evil (1974), is widely credited with showing that the strict logical contradiction doesn't hold, which is why most who press the problem today press the evidential form.

But the deepest form of the problem isn't an argument. It's a wound. Ivan Karamazov grants that the logic might work out and still hands back his ticket. Ask the group which form actually keeps people awake at night. The discipline of this session is to hold both: to know that the strict contradiction doesn't hold, and to refuse to let that abstract relief stand in for real comfort, which the rest of the study finds not in an argument but in a God who entered the suffering himself.

sessions.title: The God Who Permits
sessions.aim: To hold the doctrine of providence truthfully, that a good and sovereign God permits what he hates and works it toward an end we can't see from inside it, without a tidy resolution that makes evil acceptable, and to name plainly where the mystery remains.
sessions.summary:
Scripture doesn't teach a God who is helpless before evil, or a God who authors it, but a God who permits what he hates and bends it, against its own intent, toward an end. The strong suspicion is that "permits" is a weasel word: an all-powerful God who allows what he could stop seems as responsible as one who caused it. That suspicion deserves its full weight, and providence isn't a clean machine where every horror has a visible purpose. Saying that has wounded countless sufferers.

What the Bible gives instead comes from Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers and later raised up to save them: "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Two real intentions run through one event, and Joseph names both without collapsing either. The brothers' evil was really evil. God's good was really good. Providence isn't the claim that everything is good or that we can read God's purpose off our suffering. It's the claim that no evil escapes God's reach. And Joseph said it in hindsight. Most of us live in the pit chapters, not the throne chapter.

keyScripture.why: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today" (Genesis 50:20). Joseph names real evil done by his brothers and real good worked by God in the same event, without softening either. It's the nearest thing Scripture has to a doctrine of providence spoken by a sufferer.

discussion.q: Scripture says God permits evil he hates. Does "permits" sound to you like a real distinction, or like a word that keeps God's hands clean when he could have stopped it?
discussion.behind: Name the objection directly rather than assuming the room accepts the word. Let the difficulty be felt before any answer, so no one receives a glib distinction they haven't earned. Hold the suspicion long enough that it's real, then move to Joseph.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 50:15-21. Joseph says, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." Why does it matter that he names both and doesn't collapse one into the other?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel two intentions held together. The brothers' act was evil, not a disguised kindness. God's good was real, not an excuse for the evil. Providence doesn't baptize evil as secretly good, which is the cheap move. It says God can bend even real evil toward an end.

discussion.q: Joseph spoke that verse years later, looking back. In the pit and in prison he didn't have it. Where are you right now, the pit or the throne? What does it do to the verse to remember it was spoken in hindsight?
discussion.behind: This is the pastoral center. We quote Genesis 50:20 to people still in the pit as though they should already see the good. The verse is hindsight, a testimony Joseph could only give later, and demanding that sufferers produce it in the moment is cruelty dressed as faith. Go tenderly.

discussion.q: There's a difference between saying God works good out of evil and saying the evil was therefore good, or necessary, or a blessing in disguise. Where have you seen that line crossed, and what did it do?
discussion.behind: This line protects the sufferer. Romans 8:28 says that for those who love God all things work together for good; it doesn't say all things are good. Expose the false comfort that calls the cancer a gift or the abuse part of God's plan. Providence never asks us to call evil good.

discussion.q: Where have you felt pressure, from others or from yourself, to come up with a tidy reason for a loss? What would it free you to admit you can't see one?
discussion.behind: Close by turning to ourselves and to the mystery. Release people from the burden of manufacturing meaning they don't have. Admitting we can't see the purpose isn't a failure of faith but a truthful form of it, trusting a God we can't currently read.

objections.objection: "Permits" is a meaningless distinction. If I watched a man drown a child in a shallow pool and did nothing when I could easily have stopped it, no court would let me off because I only permitted it. An all-powerful God who permits what he could prevent is as guilty as one who does it. You're hiding behind a word.
objections.response: Used carelessly, the word becomes exactly that dodge, so it needs to be used carefully. The claim isn't that permission makes God indifferent to the suffering. It's that your courtroom example leaves out a category. The bystander at the pool gains nothing, intends nothing, and has no power to redeem the death he allows, which is why we condemn him. The claim of providence is that God doesn't idly watch, but permits only what he's able to weave toward an end that couldn't come another way, and that he himself enters and bears it. That's different from the bystander, who is simply absent. Whether it's enough is a fair fight, and the question isn't closed, because from inside the suffering it often doesn't feel like enough. But the analogy fails at the point that matters most. The God of the Bible isn't the man standing dry beside the pool. As the rest of this study will show, he's the one who climbs into the water.

objections.objection: Joseph got a happy ending. He could say God meant it for good because he ended up running Egypt. Most suffering doesn't resolve like that. The child still dies, the marriage still ends, and there's no throne where it all makes sense. Joseph is a survivor telling a survivor's story.
objections.response: This is the most searching objection to Genesis 50, and it shouldn't be waved away, because most of us live in the pit chapters and the Bible knows it. So notice what the study doesn't claim. It doesn't claim every sufferer will be given Joseph's hindsight, a clear view of the good their suffering served. Many won't be, this side of death, and promising otherwise would be a lie. What Joseph's words establish isn't that you'll see the resolution but that there is a God who can work one, that evil isn't the final author of your story even when you can't read the next chapter. Job never got an explanation, and Paul's thorn was never removed. The claim isn't "you'll understand." It's that God's reach is longer than the reach of the evil done to you, and for the Christian the throne chapter may lie on the far side of the resurrection rather than this side of the grave. That's a harder hope than Joseph's, and the study has to say so.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you been told to find the good in a loss before you were ready? What would it mean to let God hold the meaning of it for now, unseen?
sessions.practice: This week, take one hard thing from your past, far enough back that you can look at it with some distance, and do two things with it, in order. First, name the evil or the loss as real, plainly, without rushing to redeem it or calling it secretly good. Then, and only then, ask whether you can see any good God has brought out of it since, not to justify it but to trace his reach. If you can see some, give thanks for the good without blessing the evil. If you can't, tell God so, and leave the meaning with him rather than making one up. Write down which it was, and what it was like to hold the evil and the hope without collapsing one into the other.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we've been handed a hard thing tonight, that you permit what you hate, and we don't fully understand it, and we won't pretend we do. We confess we've used the word providence as a club, telling broken people to find the good before they could even breathe. Forgive us. Teach us to be like Joseph, who looked at the brothers who sold him and called their act evil to their faces, and in the same breath trusted that you'd been at work in it for good. Where we're still in the pit, and many of us are, give us patience to leave the meaning with you, unseen, rather than forcing one we don't have. We don't trust that we can read your purpose. We trust that you're good and your reach is long. Amen.
reflection: Where am I tempted to call an evil secretly good so I can feel better about it, when Scripture only claims God can work good out of it?
Am I in the pit or on the throne right now, and have I been demanding of myself a hindsight I haven't been given yet?
What would it free in me to admit I can't see God's purpose in a particular suffering, and to leave its meaning in his hands?
sessions.teaching:
Last week we let the question be as large as it is and refused every answer that survives by quietly giving up one of the three claims. Tonight we ask what the Bible actually says about God and the things that happen, and I'll warn you that its answer is stranger and harder than either side expects. The skeptic expects a tyrant who decrees every horror, and some Christians have preached exactly that. The comfortable believer expects a God who always steps in to stop bad things, and then is bewildered when he doesn't. Scripture teaches neither. It teaches a God who permits what he hates and bends it, against its own intent, toward an end.

The moment I say "permits," an objection should rise in you. If a man stands beside a shallow pool and watches a child drown when he could have pulled her out, we don't excuse him because he only permitted it. We charge him. An all-powerful God who permits what he could prevent seems to be in that position, and "permits" sounds like a word for keeping God's hands clean. That's a serious objection, and a glib answer would betray everything we said last week. But I want to show you where the analogy, powerful as it is, breaks down, and to do that I'm going to take you to Joseph.

Joseph is sold into slavery by his own brothers out of jealousy, lied about, imprisoned for years on a false charge, and forgotten in a dungeon. There's no way to read that except as real evil done to an innocent man. Then, through a chain of events no human designed, he rises to become second in power in Egypt, placed to save the region, his own family included, from a famine. Years later his brothers stand in front of him, terrified that he'll finally take revenge. And Joseph says, "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today" (Genesis 50:20).

Look at exactly what he says and doesn't say. He doesn't say, "What you did wasn't really evil; it was secretly a blessing." He calls it what it was. You meant evil. The selling was evil, the lying was evil, the stolen years were a real theft. And in the same breath, without taking back a word, he says God meant it for good. Two intentions run through one event. The brothers intended harm and did harm. God intended good and did good, and the good was real: many lives saved. Joseph holds both and collapses neither.

That's the heart of what the church calls providence, and it has to be stated carefully, because the cheap version ruins it. The cheap version says everything that happens is good, or is God's perfect will, or is secretly for the best, and it has stood in front of grieving mothers and called their dead children part of a plan. That doctrine wounds, and it isn't what Joseph says. People misquote Paul the same way. He writes, "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28). He doesn't say all things are good. The evil stays evil. What's good is God's reach into it, bending it toward an end its author never intended. Even the cross works this way: Jesus was "delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God," and yet the men who crucified him were "lawless" and guilty (Acts 2:23).

So here's why the man beside the pool is the wrong picture of God. The bystander gains nothing, intends nothing, and has no power to redeem the death he allows. He's simply absent and indifferent, which is why we condemn him. The God of providence isn't absent or indifferent. He permits only what he can weave toward an end that couldn't come another way, and, as we'll see, he doesn't stand dry at the water's edge. He climbs in.

Now I have to be careful, because if I stop here this will sound tidier than it is. Joseph speaks that verse from the throne, years later, with the shape of the story finally visible. In the pit, in the slave market, in the dungeon, he didn't have it. From inside, it was betrayal and loss and injustice with no visible point. And here's what we get wrong almost every time. We take a hindsight verse and push it at people still in the pit. We tell them to find the good now, in the fresh wound, as if faith meant producing Joseph's throne-room calm from inside the dungeon. That isn't faith; it's cruelty wearing faith's clothes. Most of us, most of the time, are in the pit chapters, and many sufferings in this life never get their Genesis 50. People bury the ones they love and pray for healing that doesn't come, and they have no clean account of what good it served. I won't invent one for them. "The secret things belong to the LORD our God" (Deuteronomy 29:29).

So providence isn't a promise that you'll understand, or that you'll be given Joseph's hindsight this side of the grave. It's the claim that no evil, however real and however unredeemed it looks from the pit, escapes the reach of a God who can bend even what was meant for harm toward an end its author never intended. God's reach is longer than the reach of the evil done to you. Where you can't see the end, and often you won't, the faithful thing isn't to manufacture a meaning. It's to leave the meaning with the God you can't currently read.

But we're still missing the deepest thing, and you can feel it. Even a God who works good out of evil can sound, from inside the dungeon, like a God managing your suffering from a comfortable distance. The Bible's last word isn't management from a distance. It's a God who climbs into the pit himself. Before we get there, though, we'll spend a week with the one man in Scripture who demanded an explanation to God's face, and with the strange way God answered him, which was not to explain at all.

scriptureStudy.note: "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." Two intentions in one event, real evil by the brothers and real good by God. The clearest statement of providence in Scripture, and the model for holding both without collapsing either.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose." Paul doesn't say all things are good. He says they're worked together for good, which guards against calling the suffering itself a blessing.

"This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men." The cross is the supreme case: real evil by guilty men, and God working through it to save the world, both held at once.

"For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD." God names the gap between his purposes and our sight, which is why we often can't read his reasons from inside our suffering.

"The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Job confesses God's sovereignty over his loss without claiming to understand it, holding trust and unanswered grief together.

"The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us." Scripture draws its own line between what God has disclosed and what he hasn't, which lets us leave the unseen purpose with him.

"Though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men." Even where God is named as allowing grief, Scripture insists it doesn't come from his heart. He takes no delight in it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the old distinction between God's permitting and God's causing, which has been argued for centuries with more care than most modern conversations bring. The Reformed tradition, following the broad stream of Augustine, has often said that God ordains whatever comes to pass while being in no way the author of sin; the Westminster Confession (1646) says this in nearly those words. It holds divine sovereignty and human responsibility together as a tension to confess rather than a contradiction to dissolve. Other faithful traditions, including much of the Arminian and Wesleyan stream, put more weight on a real permission grounded in the freedom God gives his creatures, arguing that love requires the real possibility of being refused. David Bentley Hart, writing after the 2004 tsunami in The Doors of the Sea, presses hard against any picture of God as the author of evil.

State each in its strongest form. This is an open question among faithful Christians, a place where the creeds bind us to God's goodness and sovereignty but don't settle exactly how he relates to evil. The study leans toward the language of permission, because it best keeps both God's goodness and the reality of evil in view, but it doesn't claim to see the deepest workings, and it grants that a Christian holding the stronger sovereignty view has a real biblical case this study hasn't fully answered. The error in both directions is the same: a tidiness that resolves the mystery by quietly dropping something the Bible holds.

sessions.title: Job and the Whirlwind
sessions.aim: To sit inside the one book of Scripture that refuses the formula, where a blameless man suffers without cause and God answers him not with an explanation but with his presence and a flood of questions, and to feel the rebuke God gives the friends whose tidy theology defended God by accusing the sufferer.
sessions.summary:
The Bible has a whole book on the problem of evil, and what matters most about it is what it refuses to do. Job is blameless, and God says so, and then Job loses his children, his wealth, and his health for reasons he's never told. We expect the book to end with an explanation. It doesn't. God appears in a storm and never mentions the scene in heaven or explains the suffering. He asks Job questions about the foundations of the earth, the wild goat, and the storehouses of the snow. That can feel deeply unsatisfying, and the frustration deserves to be named.

But look at what the book is doing. For thirty chapters Job's friends preach a formula: suffering is punishment for sin, so if you're suffering you must have sinned. They defend God by accusing Job. At the end God is angry, not with Job, but with them, "for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The man who protested is vindicated, and the men with the tidy theology are rebuked. God doesn't give Job a reason. He gives Job himself, and Job says, "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5).

keyScripture.why: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: 'Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?... Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?'" (Job 38:1-2, 4). God answers the sufferer with his presence and a flood of questions rather than an explanation, putting Job back inside a world larger than his own accounting.

discussion.q: God never tells Job why he suffered. What did you expect the book to do, and how do you sit with the fact that it withholds the explanation we most want?
discussion.behind: Name the expectation the book refuses. We come to Job for the answer and leave without it. Help the room feel that the withholding is deliberate, not a gap, and begin to ask why God would answer a sufferer with presence rather than explanation.

discussion.q: Job's friends preach that suffering is punishment for sin, so Job must have done something. It sounds pious, even biblical. Where have you heard that formula, from others or in your own head, and what does it do to someone who's suffering?
discussion.behind: We all carry this formula. The friends aren't cartoon villains; some of what they say sounds true in another setting. Help the room see how the formula, applied to an innocent sufferer, becomes cruel, and how naturally we reach for it to make suffering feel controllable.

discussion.q: Read Job 42:1-9. God is angry not at Job, who shook his fist, but at the friends, who defended God. Why do you think God vindicates the protester and rebukes the explainers?
discussion.behind: Let the reversal land. We assume serene acceptance is the faithful response and that the friends, who never cursed God, are the safe ones. God says the opposite. Protest spoken to God's face counts as faith, and defending God by accusing the wounded is what he calls speaking wrongly of him.

discussion.q: God answers Job with questions about the sea, the stars, and wild animals. How could being put back inside a world too large for your accounting be a comfort rather than a brush-off?
discussion.behind: Help the room hear the whirlwind as mercy. The questions don't belittle Job; they enlarge him, restoring him to a creation he belongs to but doesn't run. Sometimes relief comes not as an explanation but as a recovered sense of being small inside something vast and good.

discussion.q: Where have you been one of Job's friends, defending God by explaining someone else's pain? What did it cost them?
discussion.behind: Close by turning to ourselves. Most of us have been the friend, sure we were helping, handing a formula to someone wounded. Go first. The urge to explain someone else's suffering is often about our own need for control, and presence is almost always what the person needed.

objections.objection: God's answer to Job is a power play. A grieving man asks a fair question, and God responds by listing his credentials and asking if Job can make it rain in the desert. That isn't an answer. It's the biggest one in the room shutting up the smallest.
objections.response: Read coldly, the speech can sound like that, and a careless teacher would skip past the difficulty. So read it closely, because the tone isn't what it first seems. God doesn't condemn Job for asking. At the end he says Job spoke rightly about him and the friends, who never questioned him, spoke wrongly, which is the reverse of silencing dissent. What the whirlwind does is relocate Job. It takes a man who has shrunk the universe to the size of his own case, his ledger of innocence and grievance, and widens the frame until he stands again inside a creation of astonishing scale and wildness that he didn't make and doesn't run. That isn't God saying "How dare you ask?" It's God saying that Job belongs to something far larger than his accounting of it, and that his not-knowing is the not-knowing of a creature, not the abandonment of an orphan. Job doesn't come away crushed. He says, "now my eye sees you," which is the language of a man who has been met.

objections.objection: Even if presence is the answer, it only works if you actually get the encounter. Job heard a voice from a whirlwind. I've prayed in my own catastrophe and gotten nothing, no voice, no presence, only silence. The book solves Job's problem by giving him an experience I've asked for and not received.
objections.response: That's a fair and painful question, and it's not true that everyone gets a whirlwind. But notice two things the book itself protects. First, Job didn't get the encounter on demand. He got it after chapter after chapter of silence, after his friends had run out of formulas and his own protests had run dry, so even in the book the presence comes late, through a long darkness. Second, the book is given to us so we'd have in advance what Job didn't: the knowledge that the formula is false, that the innocent do suffer, that God vindicates the one who protests to his face, and that the deepest answer is presence. We're not promised a voice from a storm. But Christians are pointed beyond Job to a fuller presence than he ever had, a God who didn't speak from a whirlwind but came in person and entered the suffering, which is next week. If silence is where you are, the book doesn't shame you. It tells you the silence isn't God's last word.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Have you ever, like Job's friends, defended God by explaining someone else's suffering? What might you have given them instead if you'd simply sat with them in it?
sessions.practice: This week, do two things on purpose. First, find one person who is suffering and be the opposite of Job's friends. Sit with them, listen, and resist every urge to explain their pain or give them a reason. If you say almost nothing, you've done well. Second, for your own suffering, read Job 38 through 41 slowly, out loud if you can, and instead of looking for an answer, let the questions about the sea and the stars and the wild animals put you back inside a creation larger than your own case. Notice whether being made small inside something vast feels like a dismissal or, strangely, like comfort. Write down what it was like to give presence instead of answers, and to receive presence instead of an explanation.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we came to Job for an answer and you gave us a whirlwind, and we're still learning that the whirlwind was the mercy. We confess we've been the friends more often than the sufferer, sure we were defending you when we were only wounding the wounded, handing out tidy reasons to people who needed us to sit down, be quiet, and stay. Forgive us. Teach us what this book teaches, that you'd rather have our honest protest than our false calm, that you vindicated the man who argued and rebuked the men who explained. Where we're suffering, we aren't asking tonight for the reason. We're asking for you. Put us back inside a world too large for our accounting, and let it be enough to know that the One who laid the foundations of the earth hasn't lost track of us. Amen.
reflection: Where do I carry the friends' formula, the quiet belief that suffering means someone must have sinned, and how has it made me a worse comforter and a harder sufferer?
Why does God vindicate Job's protest and rebuke the friends' careful theology, and what does that tell me about what God wants from me in my pain?
When have I needed presence more than an explanation, and have I given that to others, or do I rush to explain because silence makes me uncomfortable?
sessions.teaching:
There's a whole book of the Bible on the question we've been asking, and the most important thing about it is what it refuses to do. Job opens by telling us something the rest of the book withholds from Job himself. He is "a blameless and upright man" (Job 1:8), one God points to with something like pride, and the catastrophe about to fall on him has nothing to do with any sin. Then, in a single day, he loses everything: his livestock, his servants, and then, in the blow that empties the world, all ten of his children, killed when the house collapses. Later his health goes too, and he sits in ashes scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery. And hold on to this: Job never finds out why. The reader sees the scene in heaven at the start, but Job doesn't, and inside the book he's never told the reason.

We come to Job expecting the explanation, the reason that makes suffering bearable. God does finally appear, in a storm, and you lean in. Here it comes. And he doesn't give one. He doesn't mention the scene in heaven. He doesn't say, "Job, here's what this was for." He asks questions, four chapters of them. "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" (Job 38:4). "Have you commanded the morning since your days began?" (38:12). "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion?" (38:31). The sea, the stars, the storehouses of the snow, the wild animals no one can tame. Not one word about Job's loss. And the reader thinks, that isn't an answer. I want to sit in that frustration with you, because it's real. Then I want to show you what the book is doing, because it's deeper than the explanation we wanted.

To see it, look at the friends. When they first come, they do the wisest thing anyone does in the whole book: "they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great" (Job 2:13). Then they open their mouths, and out comes the formula. God is just. He rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked. So suffering is punishment for sin, and if you're suffering like this, Job, you must have sinned, and the faithful thing is to confess it. They say it gently at first and then with growing force, and what makes it awful is that it sounds pious. Pieces of it would be fine in another setting. They're defending God. And Job, who knows he hasn't earned this, refuses the formula and does something that ought to startle us: he demands an audience. "Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face" (Job 13:15). He doesn't do what his wife suggests, "Curse God and die" (2:9), but he brings his rage and confusion straight to God and demands an answer.

Then comes the hinge of the whole book. When God finishes his questions, he turns to the friends, and he's angry. "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The men who defended God, who never questioned him, who taught careful theology about sin and punishment, spoke wrongly about him. The man who argued and protested spoke rightly. And God sends the friends to Job to ask him to pray for them. What was wrong with the friends wasn't that everything they said was false. It was that they took a general truth, that sin has consequences, and turned it into a weapon against an innocent man in agony. They made God smaller than he is and made Job's suffering his own fault. They defended God by accusing the wounded, and God won't have it.

Now go back to the whirlwind, because it reads differently once you've seen the friends rebuked. God isn't doing to Job what the friends did, crushing him with superior force. In his agony Job has shrunk the universe to the size of his own case, until the whole cosmos is a courtroom: Job against God. By asking about the foundations of the earth and the wild goat and the Pleiades, God enlarges the frame. He puts Job back inside a creation of astonishing scale and wildness and beauty, full of things that have nothing to do with Job, things God delights in for their own sake. He isn't saying, how dare you ask. He's telling Job he belongs to something far larger than his accounting of it, and that his not-knowing is the not-knowing of a creature in a vast good world, not the abandonment of an orphan in an empty one.

The proof that it's mercy is what Job says. "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5). He got no explanation at all, and yet he says he's been given something better than he had. He had known about God; now he has seen him. The encounter was the answer. God's deepest answer to suffering isn't a reason. It's himself. Job is in the Bible partly to free you from the friends' lie that you must have done something to deserve this, and partly to free you from the demand that God owe you an explanation before you'll trust him. What God gives instead is his presence, and many who have suffered deeply and met him in it say that it's enough, not because it answers the question but because it reaches the loneliness under the question, which was always the worst part.

And we have to put ourselves in this book, because most of us have been all three people in it. We've been Job, raging at a silence we couldn't understand. We've needed presence far more than an answer. And we've been the friends, sitting across from someone in agony and handing them a formula, sure we were defending God when we were only adding to the wound, because their suffering made us uncomfortable and an explanation let us feel in control. The book is a warning to everyone who rushes to explain another person's pain. Sit down. Be quiet. Stay. Give them your presence, which is what God gave Job, and stop defending God, who can defend himself and would rather have your honest grief than your false calm.

We've come a long way. But there's one more thing, the deepest thing, and Job never got to see it. Job heard a voice from a storm. We've seen a God who didn't stay outside the suffering calling out from a whirlwind, but came all the way down into it, into a body, into the dark, onto a cross. That's next week, and it's the center of everything.

scriptureStudy.note: "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?" God declares Job innocent before the suffering starts, which undoes the friends' formula in advance. The righteous do suffer without cause.

"They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great." The friends' wisest act is silent presence, before they ruin it by talking. Being with a sufferer outranks explaining to them.

"Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face." Job holds trust and protest together, refusing both to curse God and to accept the friends' formula. This is the posture God later vindicates.

"Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind... Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God answers with presence and questions rather than an explanation, putting Job back inside a creation larger than his own case.
"I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you." Job's response isn't the satisfaction of an explanation but the deeper rest of having seen God.

"My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has." God rebukes the friends' tidy theology and vindicates Job's protest, reversing our assumptions about faithful suffering.

"They showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him." The book calls it evil and still places it under God's hand, holding the reality of the evil and God's sovereignty together without resolving the tension.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how Job dismantles what scholars call the doctrine of retribution, the old and widespread assumption that prosperity rewards righteousness and suffering punishes sin. In its ordinary form that idea runs through much of the wisdom literature, that wise and righteous living tends toward flourishing, and there's real truth in it. Job marks the limit of that truth. When the general pattern is turned into an iron law and applied to an innocent sufferer, it becomes a lie and a cruelty. Notice that the friends say things that would be fine in another setting, which is what makes the book unsettling: true statements can be used falsely against a suffering person.

Set that beside John 9. The disciples see a man born blind and ask, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" That's the friends' logic exactly. Jesus answers, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him" (John 9:2-3), and breaks the formula as firmly as Job does. The discipline here is twofold. Give up the hidden arithmetic most of us carry, the quiet sense that our own suffering must be punishment and someone else's must be deserved. And learn from the friends' failure that a comforter's calling isn't to account for suffering but to share it.

sessions.title: The Crucified God
sessions.aim: To arrive at the center of the Christian answer to suffering, that the God who permits suffering didn't stay outside it but entered it himself, in a body, on a cross, so that the deepest word God speaks into human pain isn't an explanation from a safe distance but his presence inside it.
sessions.summary:
Most religions and philosophies keep their god at a distance from suffering, untouched and serene. The Christian claim is the strange one: the God who permits suffering came down into it himself. A suffering God doesn't solve the logical problem of evil any better than an untouched one, and that should be granted. But it answers the deeper wound under the argument, which is loneliness, the sense that we suffer in an empty universe under a God who watches from a height and feels nothing. On the cross God entered betrayal, injustice, agony, and abandonment, and prayed the very question of this study: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46).

The skeptic says a suffering God is a sad story we tell so we don't feel alone, with no power to fix anything. There's truth in that, if the story ended at the cross. But Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison before his execution, came to believe that "only the suffering God can help." The cross doesn't explain your suffering. It tells you that whatever pit you're in, God has been there before you, as one of the crucified, and that the One who entered the grave walked back out of it.

keyScripture.why: "He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief... Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3-4). The prophet pictures a servant who doesn't stand above suffering but takes it into himself. At the cross, God in human flesh entered it, so that his deepest word into our pain is his own presence inside it.

discussion.q: Most pictures of God keep him serene and untouched. The Christian claim is that God entered suffering on a cross. When you sit with that, what does it stir in you? Is it a comfort or a scandal?
discussion.behind: Start with the strangeness of a crucified God. For some it's the most moving thing in the faith; to a skeptic it can seem absurd or weak. Bring out the real reactions, and begin to feel that a God who enters suffering is a different kind of God from the distant watcher most people assume.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 27:45-50. On the cross Jesus prays the question of this whole study. What does it do to your own why to know that God in human flesh prayed it too?
discussion.behind: Connect the cry from the cross to the room's own questions. The why of session one isn't foreign to God; he prayed it. The question isn't outside the faith but at its center, which means the person asking it is in the deepest company there is.

discussion.q: The skeptic says a suffering God is a sad story we tell so we don't feel alone, with no power to fix anything. What's true in that, and where does it misread what the cross claims?
discussion.behind: Grant the objection its strength before answering. A suffering God doesn't solve the logical problem. But it answers the deeper wound of loneliness, and the cross isn't the end of the story. An empty tomb follows, which the objection leaves out.

discussion.q: Bonhoeffer, writing from prison before the Nazis executed him, said, "only the suffering God can help." What do you think a man in that situation meant? Why might he find more help in a God who suffers than in a God of sheer power?
discussion.behind: Let the room sit with where Bonhoeffer was. A man facing execution finding help not in divine power but in divine suffering is striking. For someone actually in the pit, a God who is present in the suffering may be more help than a distant God of might who might or might not step in.

discussion.q: Where in your own pain would it change something to know that God has been in that kind of dark before you, not as a visitor but as one of the crucified?
discussion.behind: Close by bringing it home. Help people find the specific pain where the companionship of a suffering God lands. Go first. Help the room feel the difference between a suffering explained and a suffering shared, because shared is what the cross offers.

objections.objection: A suffering God is a nice story, but that's all it is. It's consoling to imagine God hurts with us, but it doesn't change anything. The child still has cancer. A god who suffers alongside me but doesn't stop my suffering is a sympathetic spectator, not a savior. Sympathy isn't rescue.
objections.response: The first half of that is right. A God who only suffered alongside us and did nothing more would be a consolation, not a rescue; sympathy without power is company in the dark and nothing else. But the cross doesn't claim merely that God feels our pain. It claims God entered our suffering in order to defeat it from the inside, that the cross isn't the end of the story but its turning point, and that three days later the tomb was empty. The crucified God isn't a spectator who stays crucified. He took the worst suffering and death could do, died a real death, and walked out of the grave, so he didn't only sit with us in the dark; he broke it open from the inside. The cancer is real, and no one should minimize it. But Easter claims that death, the thing all suffering finally threatens, has been beaten by a God who went through it and came back. You're right that sympathy isn't rescue. This is sympathy that ends in an empty tomb, which is next week.

objections.objection: If Jesus is God, his suffering wasn't real suffering, because he knew he'd rise. He knew it would be over in three days. That's not like my suffering, where there's no guarantee and no exit in view. His was a temporary inconvenience with a happy ending he could see coming.
objections.response: This is serious, because if Christ's suffering were play-acting with a known happy ending, it would be no real solidarity at all. So look at the Gospels, which go out of their way to show the opposite. In Gethsemane Jesus is so overwhelmed that he falls on his face and asks the Father three times for another way (Matthew 26:39-44); Luke says "his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts, as the ESV notes, though Mark and Matthew describe the same anguish). That isn't the prayer of a man breezing through an inconvenience. And on the cross he doesn't pray a confident psalm of vindication. He cries, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46), the words of a man experiencing real abandonment. However the divine and human natures held together in him, the Gospels insist his anguish was total and his sense of being forsaken was real. As far as that cry shows, he suffered inside the same darkness you know. He didn't skip the dark. He went all the way into it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What dark are you in right now? What would change if you believed God had been in that kind of place before you, as one of the crucified and not as a visitor?
sessions.practice: This week, take the cry from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", and sit with it as God's own prayer in your suffering. Once, read Matthew 26 and 27 slowly, not as a familiar story but as the record of God entering the kind of dark you've known: betrayal, injustice, abandonment. Then bring your own suffering to God, not asking him to explain it this time, but telling him you know he's been here, and asking him to be present in it as the One who has. Write down whether knowing God has been in the dark changes the dark, even when it doesn't change the circumstances, and what it's like to have company there instead of an answer.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we've spent weeks asking where you are when it hurts, and tonight the answer is almost too much to take in: you aren't above the hurt, watching from a height, but inside it, on a cross, with nails through your hands and the cry of our own abandonment on your lips. We didn't expect a God who bled. We expected one who explained, or one who fixed things, or one who stayed out of reach. Instead you came down into the worst of it, the betrayal, the injustice, the dark, the forsakenness, and you didn't skip any of it. We don't fully understand what it means that God suffered. But we understand that we aren't alone in the pit, because you've been in it, and that changes the pit. Be present in our suffering as the One who has been here. And remind us, when we get there next, that the cross wasn't the end of your story. Amen.
reflection: What picture of God have I carried, a distant watcher or a God who entered suffering, and how has it shaped whether I bring my pain to him or carry it alone?
Jesus prayed the why of forsakenness from the cross. What does that do to my own unanswered why?
Where would it change something, not the circumstances but the loneliness, to believe God has been in my kind of dark before me?
sessions.teaching:
We've come to the center now, and everything so far has been clearing the ground for it. We stated the question at full strength. We saw that God permits what he hates and bends it toward an end we usually can't see, and that his answer to Job wasn't an explanation but his presence. Now we come to what makes the Christian account of suffering different from every other one, something a skeptic couldn't have predicted.

Every religion and philosophy has to do something with suffering, and almost all of them keep God at a safe distance from it. The god of the philosophers is serene and untouched, beyond change and so beyond pain. Many spiritual paths counsel detachment, escaping suffering by ceasing to desire. And many unbelievers conclude that there's no one up there at all and we suffer alone under an empty sky. Then there's the Christian claim, which the ancient world found offensive, the kind of thing nobody would invent. The God who permits suffering didn't stay outside it. "Though he was in the form of God," he "emptied himself... becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:6-8). He took a body that could be beaten and a heart that could be broken, and he went to the bottom of human suffering, to a Roman cross, one of the most agonizing and humiliating deaths the ancient world devised.

I have to be careful about what this does and doesn't do, because if I oversell it I'll lose the skeptic, and the skeptic is the reader I most want to be fair to. A suffering God doesn't, by itself, solve the logical problem of evil. If you came for a tighter argument, this isn't it. But the logical problem was never the deepest part of the wound. For most people in real suffering, the deepest part is loneliness, the sense of suffering alone in the dark under a God who, if he exists, is watching from a comfortable height and feeling nothing. That's what breaks people. And that's exactly the wound the cross goes to.

Look at what God entered. Not a tidy, symbolic suffering, but the real thing. He was betrayed by a friend for thirty pieces of silver, deserted by the people closest to him, condemned though innocent, mocked, beaten, and nailed to a cross, left to die slowly with his mother watching. And at the end he cried out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Do you hear what that is? It's the question. It's the why of session one, the "how long" and "where are you" of the Psalms, prayed at the bottom of everything by God in human flesh. The question we worried might be a failure of faith to ask was prayed by the Son of God in the darkest hour there has been. When you ask it, you aren't standing outside the faith shaking your fist at it. You're in the deepest company there is.

The skeptic has a sharp reply, and it deserves to be stated well. A suffering God, he says, is a sad story we tell ourselves so we don't feel alone. It's consoling, but it changes nothing. The child still has cancer. A god who suffers with me but doesn't stop my suffering is a sympathetic spectator, and sympathy isn't rescue. I grant the second half entirely. A God who only suffered with us and did nothing else would be company in the dark and no more. But the cross doesn't claim only that God feels our pain from beside us. It claims he entered suffering to defeat it from the inside, that the cross is the turning point of a longer story, and that the One who went into the grave didn't stay there. We'll get to the empty tomb next week. Hold this much tonight: the crucified God isn't a spectator who stays crucified.

There's a second objection, just as serious. If Jesus is God, his suffering wasn't like mine, because he knew he'd rise. But look at the Gospels, which go out of their way to show otherwise. In Gethsemane, the night before he died, he fell on his face and asked the Father three times for another way. Luke says that "being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44; some early manuscripts lack the verse, but Mark and Matthew describe the same anguish). On the cross he didn't pray a serene psalm of vindication. He cried out as a man abandoned. However the divine and human held together in him, a mystery the church has handled carefully for twenty centuries, the Gospels insist his anguish was real. He didn't skip the dark. He went all the way into it. "We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses," Hebrews says, "but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15).

I want you to meet one witness tonight. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German pastor and theologian who opposed Hitler's regime, was arrested in 1943, and was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp in April 1945, weeks before the war in Europe ended. From his cell he wrote letters, later published as Letters and Papers from Prison, and in one of them he wrote, "only the suffering God can help." He had come to believe that the Bible directs us not first to God's power in the world, the strong arm we keep begging to step in, but to God's weakness and suffering, the God who is with us by suffering with us. Think about who said that, and from where. A man in a Nazi prison, with every reason to want a God of overwhelming power to break him out, found that what he could lean his whole weight on was a God who had been in cells and on crosses himself. That's testimony from a prison, not an armchair.

So the cross doesn't explain your suffering. I told you in the first session I wouldn't hand you an explanation, and I'm keeping that promise here at the center. The cross does something an explanation never could. It tells you that whatever pit you're in, however dark and lonely, God has been there before you, not as a visitor who stopped in and left, but as one of the crucified, who knew betrayal and injustice and physical agony and even the felt absence of God. You don't suffer alone. The sky isn't empty, and the One above it isn't untouched. He came down. And the skeptic is right that this companionship wouldn't be enough if it ended there. It doesn't end there. Next week we go to the morning when the dark of the cross didn't get the last word, to the empty tomb, where suffering meets not an explanation but a defeat.

scriptureStudy.note: "A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief... Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows." The prophet's portrait of a servant who doesn't stand above suffering but takes it into himself, fulfilled at the cross.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Jesus prays the cry of the abandoned from Psalm 22, taking the sufferer's why into the experience of God in human flesh.

"And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground." Some early manuscripts lack this verse, but Mark 14:33-34 shows the same distress. Christ's suffering was real dread, not painless certainty.

"For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin." The God we approach isn't distant from human weakness. He has entered it, which is why we can draw near in pain.
"For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted." Christ's own suffering is named as what equips him to help the suffering.
"Though he was in the form of God... he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross." God was under no obligation to suffer and chose the lowest place.
"Jesus wept." At his friend's grave, knowing he would raise him, Jesus still weeps with the grieving. He doesn't stand above sorrow even when he holds the power to undo it.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the doctrine of divine impassibility and the long argument over whether and how God suffers. Faithful believers stand on both sides. The classical tradition, drawing on the church fathers, has generally held that God in his divine nature is impassible, not subject to suffering or acted on from outside, to protect the truth that God isn't a victim swept along by forces greater than himself. On this reading Christ's suffering is real but borne in his human nature: the eternal Son truly experiences human suffering through the incarnation without the divine nature being diminished. A strong modern stream, writing in the shadow of the twentieth century's atrocities, has argued instead that the cross reveals a God who takes pain into his own life. Jürgen Moltmann gave this its most influential form in The Crucified God (1972; English 1974).

State both carefully. The creeds bind us to the full deity and full humanity of Christ and to the reality of the cross, and leave the exact metaphysics of divine suffering more open than either side sometimes admits. The study rests on the pastoral ground both share: in Christ, God truly entered human suffering, and there's now no human pit he hasn't known from the inside. Set Bonhoeffer's prison letters beside this, and ask how a man facing execution could find help in a suffering God.
