sessions.title: Hope That Does Not Disappoint
sessions.aim: To end the study where Christian hope lands, not in an explanation of suffering but in its final defeat, the resurrection of Christ and the new creation where every tear is wiped away, so that suffering is neither minimized nor explained away but named as real and then as not the last word.
sessions.summary:
For five weeks we've refused to explain suffering away, and we won't start now. Christian hope isn't that suffering was secretly fine, or that it all made sense in the end, or even that you'll understand it someday. It's that suffering, real and terrible and unexplained, will be defeated. The strong suspicion is that heaven is the oldest trick there is, a promise that can't be checked, used to keep suffering people quiet. It has been misused exactly that way. But Christian hope rests on an event: the resurrection of Jesus, the morning the cross didn't get the last word.

Paul writes that "the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18), and he wrote it as a man who had been beaten, stoned, shipwrecked, and imprisoned. The whole creation groans "in the pains of childbirth" (Romans 8:22), real agony that is producing something. And the Bible ends with God himself dwelling with his people: "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4). Not suffering explained. Suffering ended, by the hand of God.

keyScripture.why: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man... He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:3-4). The Bible's last word on suffering isn't an explanation but a defeat, every tear wiped away by God himself.

discussion.q: Christian hope isn't that suffering made sense but that it will be defeated. What's the difference between a suffering explained and a suffering defeated? Which have you actually been longing for?
discussion.behind: Distinguish the two hopes. We often think we want the explanation, but the deeper longing is usually for the suffering to be ended and undone. The gospel offers the second, and defeat is a larger hope than understanding.

discussion.q: The skeptic says heaven is pie in the sky, a reward that can't be checked, used to keep the suffering quiet. Where has the church earned that criticism? Where does it misread what Christian hope rests on?
discussion.behind: Grant the objection fully first. The church has used heaven to pacify the oppressed, and that abuse is real. Then notice that Christian hope rests on a claimed event, the resurrection, rather than an uncheckable promise, and that it has often fueled the fight against injustice rather than only sedating it.

discussion.q: Read Romans 8:18-25 and 2 Corinthians 11:23-28. Paul says present sufferings aren't worth comparing with the coming glory, and he says it as a man who had been beaten, stoned, and shipwrecked. Does it change the line to know who said it?
discussion.behind: Ground the hope in the witness. The line sounds glib from a comfortable person and weighty from a sufferer. Paul isn't waving suffering away from a distance; he's weighing it from inside, which makes his judgment tested rather than cheap.

discussion.q: Revelation says God himself will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Sit with that picture, God's own hand on your face. What does it offer that an end to suffering, or an explanation of it, wouldn't?
discussion.behind: Let the room stay with the tenderness of it. It isn't only that suffering ends, but that God personally attends to each person who grieves. The final answer to suffering isn't a cosmic mechanism but a Father's hand on a wet face.

discussion.q: After five weeks, where do you land, and what will you carry from this study into your own unanswered suffering?
discussion.behind: Close the study without forcing a resolution. Let people name where they are, doubt included, and what they're taking with them. Go first. End with weight and hope held together, and no pressure to have arrived anywhere in particular.

objections.objection: Heaven is the oldest trick in the book. Promise suffering people a reward they can't verify, after they're dead, so they'll endure their misery quietly instead of demanding justice now. It's an opiate. The powerful have always loved a religion that tells the suffering to wait for the next life.
objections.response: That criticism has been earned again and again. The promise of heaven has been used as an opiate, to tell slaves to obey their masters and the oppressed to wait quietly, and Christians have to own that rather than dodge it. But the criticism misses two things. First, resurrection hope isn't an uncheckable promise floated to pacify people. It rests on a claimed event in history, the empty tomb, which the first witnesses kept proclaiming at great cost, and which you can investigate rather than dismiss as wishful thinking. Second, against the opiate charge directly, resurrection hope has fueled the fight against injustice at least as often as it has sedated it, because people who believe evil will finally be judged and that their resistance isn't futile are freed to confront it now without despair. The same hope that comforts the dying has sent reformers and martyrs to stand in front of tyrants. Hoping the dark won't have the last word doesn't mean accepting the dark. It can mean fighting it with confidence. The opiate is an abuse of the hope, not the hope itself.

objections.objection: Even if there's a new creation where every tear is wiped away, that doesn't undo the suffering that already happened. The child who died in agony still died in agony. A future where it stops doesn't reach back and unmake the past.
objections.response: This is the deepest objection of all, and it's not true that the future simply erases the past. The resurrection itself refuses that. The risen Christ still bears his wounds. He tells Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands" (John 20:27). The wounds weren't deleted. They were healed, and now they're the proof of his love rather than only the marks of his torture. So Christian hope isn't amnesia, a future that acts as if the past horror was nothing. The New Testament points toward a redemption deep enough to reach backward, where the very places we were broken somehow become places of glory, but it doesn't spell out how. Anyone who claims to have that mapped is overreaching. This is the strongest objection the study hasn't fully answered, and it's named as that. What it can offer is the scarred and risen Christ, whose worst day became the turning point of the world's salvation, as ground for trusting that the tears already shed won't merely be stopped but somehow gathered up and answered by a God who doesn't forget them and doesn't waste them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you believed that the suffering you carry will one day be not explained but defeated, and that God himself will wipe the tears from your face, what would you dare to hope for that you've stopped letting yourself hope for?
sessions.practice: This week, hold both halves of Christian hope together on purpose. First, don't minimize your suffering. Name it as real and let it be as heavy as it is. Then read Revelation 21 and Romans 8:18-25 slowly, and let yourself picture the promise concretely: not suffering explained but suffering ended, God's own hand on your face, the particular grief you carry undone. Sit in the tension of a real present grief and a real future hope without collapsing either. If you've stopped hoping because hope kept disappointing you, bring even that to God. Write down what it's like to grieve and hope at the same time, and whether the empty tomb gives you ground that wishful thinking wouldn't.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, we've asked for five weeks where you are when it hurts, and you haven't given us a tidy answer, and we've found we don't need one as badly as we thought. We've found that you permit what you hate and bend it past the ones who meant it for harm. We've found that you answer the sufferer with your presence. We've found that you didn't stay above the pain but came into it on a cross. And now we find that the cross wasn't the end, that the tomb is empty, that the dark you entered you also defeated. We still grieve, and you don't ask us to stop, because the tears are real and you don't pretend otherwise. But you've promised to wipe them away, every one, with your own hand, and to make an end of death and mourning and crying and pain. We'll carry that out of this room. Not suffering explained. Suffering defeated. And until that morning, your presence in the dark, which has turned out to be enough. Amen.
reflection: Have I been longing for my suffering to be explained, when the deeper hope on offer is for it to be defeated? What changes if I let myself want the larger thing?
Where has the promise of future hope been used to silence me or others, and how is resurrection hope different from the opiate the skeptic rightly rejects?
If God himself will one day wipe the tears from my face, how does that promise change the way I carry an unhealed grief now?
sessions.teaching:
For five weeks I've refused to explain suffering away, and I won't break that promise in the last session, even though this is where you might expect the resolution. It isn't coming, not the airtight account you might have wanted in week one. Christian hope isn't that suffering was secretly fine, or that it all clicked into place, or even that you'll understand it someday. It's stranger and stronger than understanding. It's that suffering, real and terrible and unexplained, is going to be defeated. An explanation would tell you why the child died. A defeat undoes the death. We keep asking God for the small thing, the explanation, when what he has promised is the enormous thing: not that suffering will be justified but that it will be destroyed.

The moment I say "hope," a fair suspicion should rise, and it's the skeptic's strongest card. Heaven, he says, is the oldest trick in the book: promise suffering people a reward after they're safely dead, where nobody can check, so they'll endure their misery quietly instead of demanding justice. It's the charge Karl Marx made famous, that religion is an opiate, and the powerful have always liked a religion that keeps the suffering docile. I'm not going to dodge it, because it's true that heaven has been used that way. Slaveholders preached heaven to enslaved people to keep them obedient. That's a real abuse, and Christians have to own it.

But here's what the abuse misses. Christian hope isn't a vague optimism floated to pacify people. It rests on a claimed event, in a particular place, on a particular morning. The tomb was empty. The God who entered death on Friday walked out of it on Sunday, and the first Christians didn't preach a comforting idea. They proclaimed something they insisted they had seen, and they kept proclaiming it through beatings, prison, and, by early tradition, death. You can investigate that claim, and it's different from wishful thinking, because wishful thinking doesn't usually hold up under that kind of cost. And against the opiate charge directly, the belief that suffering will be defeated and every injustice finally judged has often set people on fire to fight injustice now. If you believe the dark isn't the last word, you're free to confront it without despair. The same hope that comforts the dying has sent reformers and martyrs to stand in front of tyrants.

Who says a thing about suffering matters as much as what's said; we learned that with Bonhoeffer. Paul writes, "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). Read flat, that sounds glib. But consider who wrote it. Elsewhere Paul lists what his faith cost him: "Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked" (2 Corinthians 11:24-25), and early tradition says he was finally executed in Rome. This isn't someone waving suffering off from a distance. It's a man who suffered more than almost anyone in this room will, weighing his own real agony against what he believed was coming, and saying the suffering doesn't tip the scale against the glory. That's a tested judgment.

And Paul gives the broken world an image that honors suffering while pointing past it. "For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:22). Labor pains are real, severe agony, and Paul doesn't pretend otherwise. But they're the pains of birth, not death. The suffering is real, and it isn't pointless thrashing in the dark. It's labor, and a child is coming.

So where does this study land? In the last pages of the Bible, in what John was shown. "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away" (Revelation 21:3-4). Notice what it is and what it isn't. It isn't suffering explained. There's no paragraph in Revelation that finally answers Ivan. What John is given is suffering defeated. Death is abolished. Mourning and crying and pain are ended, not justified. And notice how tender it is. God himself wipes away the tears, not some impersonal mechanism, the way a father wipes the face of a child who has cried himself out. Isaiah saw it centuries before: "the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" (Isaiah 25:8). The final answer to the suffering of the world was never an argument, all the way back to Job. It's a Person, and a hand, and a face, and the end of every tear.

I owe you one more piece of candor, because there's a deep objection even to this. Someone is thinking: a future where the tears are wiped away doesn't undo the tears already shed. The child still died in agony. That's the strongest objection I know, and I can't fully answer it. But Scripture gives one hint. When Jesus rose, he still had his wounds. He showed Thomas the marks in his hands and side (John 20:27). The wounds weren't deleted, as if the suffering had never happened. They were healed and still there, and they had become the proof of his love rather than only the marks of his torture. That suggests the new creation isn't amnesia. It suggests a redemption deep enough to reach backward, where the places we were broken become, in a way I can't map and won't pretend to, the places where love and victory show most clearly. I'd rather leave you with a true mystery than a false closure.

So we end where we began, with the question still standing, and everything changed. The Bible never gives the explanation, and I won't invent what God withheld. What it gives is a God who permits what he hates and bends it past the ones who meant it for harm, who answers the sufferer with his presence, who came all the way down into the pain onto a cross, and who walked out of the grave on the third day as the first light of a new creation, and has promised to wipe every tear from every face and make an end of death. That isn't the problem of evil solved. It's the problem of evil outlasted, answered not with a reason but with a Person and an empty tomb. The dark is real. But it isn't the last word. The last word belongs to the One on the throne who says, "Behold, I am making all things new" (Revelation 21:5). If tonight the grief is still heavier than the hope, you aren't behind. Bring both, and keep coming, because the One who entered the dark is the One who will end it, and he hasn't lost track of a single tear.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take seriously the charge that religion is an opiate, because it was made seriously and deserves a serious answer. In its sharpest form it says that a promised future reward drains the energy that might otherwise go into changing things now. A fair group should grant without flinching that the church has often deserved it, preaching a heaven that told the enslaved and the exploited to endure quietly.

But the historical record cuts both ways. The same resurrection hope has repeatedly fed the confrontation with injustice rather than dampening it. The movements to abolish slavery and to win civil rights drew deeply on the conviction that God will finally judge injustice and that resistance isn't futile. Set this beside the New Testament's refusal to let hope replace action: those who hope for the new creation are the ones called to live its justice now. Then weigh the difference between hope grounded in an event and hope grounded in a wish, between the resurrection as a claimed historical occurrence open to investigation and a general optimism that asks nothing and checks nothing. The discipline of this last session is to hold the hope as neither an opiate that excuses passivity nor a sedative immune to evidence, but as a tested conviction that the suffering we've refused to minimize for five weeks isn't the last word.

leaderPrimer:
Plan every session as if the wound in the room were fresh, because somewhere at your table it is. A diagnosis that came this year, a child who isn't okay, a grave with new grass on it: for that person, the providence of God isn't a topic. It's the question they cry into a pillow. Everything you say about God's sovereignty will land on their particular catastrophe, so weigh each sentence before it leaves your mouth.

The danger in this study has a name, and the name is Job's friends. They were orthodox. Most of their sentences would pass a doctrine exam. They took the true idea that God governs all things and used it to explain one man's particular agony, and at the end of the book God's anger falls on them for not speaking rightly of him, not on the sufferer who shouted his complaint at heaven (Job 42:7). You'll feel their temptation every week, because tidy sovereignty is easier to say than the true thing, which is that God permits what he hates for reasons we mostly can't see from inside it. Say the true thing. Never explain anyone's tragedy to them. Never connect their loss to a lesson, a purpose they ought to be seeing, or a hidden good you've identified on their behalf. That arithmetic belongs to God alone, and every human who attempts it wounds. What you can do is keep the room moving toward the answer Scripture finally gives, which isn't an argument but a Person with scars.

You won't resolve the question in five weeks, and neither does the study. Saying so plainly in session one will earn more trust than any argument. Expect anger at God to surface, and when it does, don't defend him. He has never asked for that, and the psalms he inspired hold more complaint than your group has yet dared (Psalm 13). Your posture to the end is the one the friends had for their first seven days: quiet, near, and unshocked. Sit closer than you explain. That's the whole assignment.

faq.q: Is this study going to give me an answer to why God allows suffering?
faq.a: No, and it says so from the first session. There's no tidy answer to the problem of evil, no paragraph that makes suffering make sense, and the study won't pretend otherwise, because the studies that pretend are the ones that wound. It takes the question at full strength, refuses the cheap answers that survive only by quietly dropping one of the three claims (that God is good, that God is able, that evil is real), and walks toward the response Scripture finally gives, which isn't an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself. You won't find the explanation that closes the case, because the Bible doesn't give it. You'll find a God who permits what he hates and bends it toward an end, who answers the sufferer with his presence, who came into the pain on a cross, and who has promised to defeat suffering rather than merely justify it.

faq.q: How is this different from the grief study or the lament study?
faq.a: They sit side by side but they aren't the same. The grief study walks through personal loss, the death of someone you love and how to carry it. The lament study teaches the prayer language of sorrow, how to bring grief to God in the words Scripture gives. This study takes the harder question underneath both, the problem of evil itself, why a good and sovereign God permits suffering at all. It's written toward the skeptic first, the person whose faith broke, or never formed, over the suffering of the innocent. If you're carrying a fresh loss, the grief and lament studies may meet you more directly. If the question that haunts you is whether a good God can be squared with a world like this, this study was built for that.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic, and the problem of evil is exactly why I can't believe. Will this study take that seriously or just try to talk me out of it?
faq.a: It's written toward you first, and it takes your objection more seriously than most believers do. The first session states the problem at full strength, including Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov, who refuses a paradise bought with the unavenged tears of a tortured child, and it grants that the objection is strong. The study won't pretend the difficulty disappears, and it won't hand you a proof. What it offers is a claim worth weighing, that the dilemma isn't as airtight as it looks, and a response that isn't an argument but a God who entered the suffering himself and walked out of the grave. You can finish still disbelieving and know you were met fairly.

faq.q: Does the study claim that everything happens for a reason?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to take that phrase apart, because it has wounded more grieving people than almost any other. Session two draws the line carefully. Scripture says God works good out of evil, in Joseph's words, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20), and in Paul's, that "for those who love God all things work together for good" (Romans 8:28). It doesn't say all things are good, or that the evil was a blessing in disguise, or that every horror has a purpose you should be able to find. Joseph calls the evil evil while trusting God worked good through it, and he says it years later, with a hindsight he didn't have in the pit. The study insists we're usually in the pit, that we often can't read God's purpose at all, and that demanding a sufferer produce a reason in the moment is cruelty dressed as faith.

faq.q: Why does the book of Job get a whole session when God never even answers Job's question?
faq.a: Because that's the point. Job is Scripture's whole book on the problem of evil, and the most significant thing about it is what it refuses to do, which is explain. Job is blameless, God says so, and he suffers terribly for reasons he's never told. When God finally answers, he gives no reason. He gives his presence and a flood of questions that put Job back inside a creation too large for his own accounting. And at the end God is angry, not at Job, who protested, but at the friends who defended God with a formula, that suffering must be punishment for sin. The protester is vindicated and the explainers are rebuked. Session three sits in that, because it frees us from the friends' lie and shows that God's deepest answer to suffering is an encounter, not an argument.

faq.q: What does it mean that God suffers? Doesn't God being God mean he's above all that?
faq.a: It's a deep and contested question, and session four handles it carefully. The classical tradition has generally held that God in his divine nature doesn't suffer, to protect the truth that he isn't a victim of forces greater than himself, and that Christ's suffering is real but borne in his human nature. A strong modern stream, written in the shadow of the twentieth century's atrocities, has argued that the cross reveals a God who takes pain into his own life. The study states both and rests on what they share, that in Christ God truly entered human suffering, so there's no human pit he hasn't known from the inside. It doesn't claim to have mapped the deeper metaphysics, which Scripture itself doesn't spell out.

faq.q: Who was Bonhoeffer, and why does the study lean on him?
faq.a: Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German pastor and theologian who opposed Hitler's regime, was imprisoned by the Nazis in 1943, and was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp in April 1945, weeks before the war in Europe ended. From his cell he wrote letters later collected as Letters and Papers from Prison, and in one of them he wrote, "only the suffering God can help," meaning that the help we need comes less from a God of sheer power than from the God who suffers alongside us. The study leans on him because of where he wrote from. A man facing execution, with every reason to want a God of overwhelming power to break him out, found that what he could lean on was a God who had been in cells and on crosses himself. That's testimony from a prison, not an armchair.

faq.q: If God just wipes away the tears later, does that really fix the suffering that already happened?
faq.a: This is the deepest objection in the study, and session five names it as the strongest one it can't fully answer. A future where suffering stops doesn't, on its face, reach back and unmake the past; the child who died in agony still died in agony. The one hint Scripture gives is the risen Christ, who still bore his wounds, healed but not erased. That suggests the new creation isn't amnesia but a redemption somehow deep enough to reach backward, where the wounds themselves become places of glory and not only loss. The study says plainly that it can't map how that works, and that anyone claiming to have it mapped is overreaching. It points to the scarred and risen Christ as ground for trusting that the tears already shed aren't lost or wasted.

faq.q: Is the hope of heaven just a way to keep suffering people quiet?
faq.a: The study grants that this criticism has been earned. The promise of heaven has been used as an opiate, telling the enslaved and the oppressed to endure quietly and wait, and Christians have to own that. But the criticism misses two things. First, resurrection hope rests on a claimed event in history, the empty tomb, which the first witnesses kept proclaiming at great cost, and which you can investigate rather than dismiss. Second, the same hope has fueled the fight against injustice at least as often as it has sedated it, because people who believe evil will finally be judged are freed to confront it now without despair. Hoping the dark won't have the last word doesn't mean accepting the dark.

faq.q: I am in fresh grief right now. Is this study going to make it worse?
faq.a: It might be too soon, and that is worth saying plainly. This study is built to take the intellectual question seriously, and if you are in the raw early weeks of a loss, the grief study or the lament study may meet you more gently and directly than this one. The study refuses at every turn to explain suffering away or to hand you a formula, which is often what makes fresh grief worse. It validates the feeling and never the despair. It protects the grieving from the room's instinct to explain their pain. And it keeps a path to real help visible, because suffering can press past what a study can hold. If you are in acute distress, please do not carry it alone, tell your group leader, a pastor, or a counselor, and if you are in danger, reach out to a crisis line and stay with someone safe. The study can wait. You matter more than finishing it.

faq.q: Why does the study keep refusing to give a clean answer? Isn't that just dodging the hard question?
faq.a: It's refusing to lie. A clean answer to the problem of evil doesn't exist, and the studies that hand one out aren't braver, only less truthful, and people who are suffering can feel it. The Bible itself withholds the explanation. Job demands one and never gets it. Jesus prays the why from the cross. What Scripture gives instead is harder and more durable: a God who permits what he hates and bends it toward an end, who answers the sufferer with his presence, who entered the pain on a cross, and who has promised to defeat suffering rather than justify it. A faith willing to keep its unanswered questions in the room is more trustworthy, especially to a skeptic, than one that pretends the case is closed.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I don't have the problem of evil figured out myself?
faq.a: Your unresolved question isn't a disqualification. No one has the problem of evil figured out, and the moment you act as though you do, you lose the room. The study is built to be led by a fellow sufferer, not an expert with answers. Every discussion question has notes on what's behind it, every objection is laid out at its strongest, and every session ends in prayer, so you won't be improvising. Your candor about your own unanswered suffering may be what frees others to stop performing certainty. What you do need is to take the skeptic's question seriously, refuse to let the group explain away real pain, protect the grieving, keep a path to real help visible, and point everyone, yourself first, to the God who entered the dark and walked back out of it.

timeline.event: Joseph is sold into slavery by his brothers and raised up to save them, later naming two intentions in one event, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good."

The book of Job is written, Scripture's whole treatment of the problem of evil, in which a blameless man suffers without explanation, his friends' formula is rebuked, and God answers out of the whirlwind with his presence rather than a reason.
The psalmists give Israel the language of complaint, "How long, O LORD?" and "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", bringing the question of God's absence straight to God without rebuke.
Epicurus is later credited with an early sharp form of the problem of evil, a God either unwilling or unable to prevent evil, a sign of how old the question is.
Jesus is betrayed, condemned, and crucified, praying from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Three days later the tomb is found empty.

Paul writes to the Romans that present sufferings aren't worth comparing with the coming glory, that creation groans in the pains of childbirth, and that for those who love God all things work together for good.
John records the vision of Revelation, the new creation where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, and death and mourning and crying and pain are no more.
Augustine describes evil as the privation of good, a corruption of what God made good rather than a thing in itself, shaping Western Christian thought about evil for over a thousand years.
Fyodor Dostoevsky publishes The Brothers Karamazov, in which Ivan refuses a final harmony bought with the unavenged suffering of a tortured child and hands back his ticket.
C. S. Lewis publishes The Problem of Pain (1940), an argument, and A Grief Observed (1961), written from inside his grief after his wife's death, refusing answers he had once found easier to give.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer, imprisoned for opposing Hitler, is hanged at Flossenbürg weeks before the war in Europe ends, having written from prison that "only the suffering God can help."

Alvin Plantinga publishes God, Freedom, and Evil, widely held to show that there's no strict logical contradiction in an all-good, all-powerful God permitting evil, and shifting the debate toward the evidential form of the problem.

facilitatorScript.open:
Welcome, and thanks for being here. This is the hardest question there is, and most of us have been told to keep quiet about it, so it takes some courage to come. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say here that you don't understand how a good God allows this. You can say you lost your faith over it, or you're barely holding on to it, or you're still angry at God about something that happened. Nobody is going to grade your faith or hand you a formula to fix your grief. Second, this study isn't going to give you a tidy answer to why God allows suffering, because there isn't one, and anyone who hands you one isn't being straight with you. We're after something harder and sturdier than an answer. Third, I'm inside this too. I have my own unanswered suffering, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. We aren't solving a puzzle from above. We're walking toward something together.

Tonight we're sitting with this part of the question: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what Scripture says here. Now let's bring it home, into the suffering we carry or watch others carry, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't. And as we do, let's be careful with each other, because someone in this room isn't discussing this in the abstract.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, and if it doesn't feel resolved, that's all right, because the problem of evil doesn't resolve on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take this into your week, try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you are carrying a grief or a doubt or a suffering that feels too heavy to hold alone, please do not carry it alone, talk to me or to someone safe. If you are in real danger or despair, tell me tonight, before you leave, because you matter more than any study. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for being in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and refusing cheap answers, and say plainly that this question drives more people from the faith than almost any other, and that it's welcome here.
Week 2: Session 1, The Question That Will Not Quiet, stating the problem at full strength, including Ivan Karamazov, and taking the skeptic's objection seriously.
Week 3: Session 2, The God Who Permits, providence and Joseph, with extended time on the difference between God working good out of evil and the evil being secretly good.
Week 4: Session 3, Job and the Whirlwind, with extended time on the rebuke of the friends and on presence over explanation.
Week 5: Session 4, part one, The Crucified God, the cross as God's entry into suffering, sitting first with the cry from the cross.
Week 6: Session 4 continued, Bonhoeffer's witness and the skeptic's reply that a suffering God is only sympathy, drawing out that the cross is followed by the empty tomb.
Week 7: Session 5, Hope That Does Not Disappoint, the resurrection and the new creation, handled so the hope doesn't minimize the grief.

Week 8: Integration. Trace the whole movement, question to providence to Job to cross to hope, revisit the five practices, and name what each person is carrying, with space and a clear path to further help for anyone needing it.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the question at full strength and the God who permits what he hates.
Week 2: Session 3, Job and the Whirlwind, with extended time on the rebuke of the friends.
Week 3: Session 4, The Crucified God, the center of the study, with Bonhoeffer's witness.
Week 4: Session 5, Hope That Does Not Disappoint, plus a short close holding grief and hope together.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, The Question That Will Not Quiet.
Week 2: Session 2, The God Who Permits.
Week 3: Session 3, Job and the Whirlwind.
Week 5: Session 5, Hope That Does Not Disappoint.

bibliography.title: The Brothers Karamazov
bibliography.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
bibliography.note: The source of Ivan's objection, the problem of evil at its most searching. Background for session 1. Read the chapter "Rebellion" (Book 5, chapter 4) in a good translation before quoting it.

bibliography.title: Letters and Papers from Prison
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written from a Nazi cell before his execution, and the source of "only the suffering God can help." The witness at the center of session 4.

bibliography.title: The Problem of Pain
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's 1940 treatment of the intellectual problem, arguing from free will and the place of pain. Background for session 1; best read alongside A Grief Observed.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Written from inside Lewis's grief after his wife's death and published in 1961, a model of grief that doesn't resolve neatly. Supports the study's refusal of cheap comfort.

bibliography.title: Where Is God When It Hurts?
bibliography.author: Philip Yancey
bibliography.note: A pastoral, readable treatment of suffering that holds the question without pretending to a tidy solution. A companion for the whole study.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Includes a chapter on suffering written toward the skeptic, granting the force of the objection while pointing to the cross and resurrection.

bibliography.title: Walking with God through Pain and Suffering
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A fuller treatment drawing together the philosophical, biblical, and pastoral sides of suffering, for leaders who want more depth on providence and the cross.

bibliography.title: The Crucified God
bibliography.author: Jürgen Moltmann
bibliography.note: The most influential modern statement of the theology of divine suffering. Background for session 4 and the debate over impassibility; one serious voice in that debate, not settled doctrine.

bibliography.title: God, Freedom, and Evil
bibliography.author: Alvin Plantinga
bibliography.note: The 1974 philosophical case widely held to show there's no strict logical contradiction between an all-good, all-powerful God and evil. Background for session 1's going deeper.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Where Augustine works out evil as the privation of good (Book 7), and the source of the restless heart that finds rest in God. Background across the study.

bibliography.title: Lament for a Son
bibliography.author: Nicholas Wolterstorff
bibliography.note: A philosopher's raw grief after the death of his son in a climbing accident, holding faith and anguish together. Useful alongside session 5.

bibliography.title: The Doors of the Sea: Where Was God in the Tsunami?
bibliography.author: David Bentley Hart
bibliography.note: A sharp argument, written after the 2004 tsunami, against making God the author of evil. A serious voice for session 2, to be weighed rather than simply adopted.

furtherReading: The Brothers Karamazov, Fyodor Dostoevsky, for readers willing to meet the problem of evil in Ivan's refusal, alongside the first session.
Letters and Papers from Prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for those who want to sit with the witness of a man who found help in the suffering God while facing execution.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone living inside a grief that doesn't resolve.
Walking with God through Pain and Suffering, Timothy Keller, for a fuller treatment holding the philosophical, biblical, and pastoral threads together.
Where Is God When It Hurts?, Philip Yancey, for a pastoral and readable companion to the question.

glossary.definition: The old and central objection that a God who is both all-good and all-powerful seems incompatible with real and terrible suffering. The study takes it at full strength and refuses every answer that dissolves it by quietly dropping one of those claims.

An attempt to justify God's goodness and power in the face of evil. The study is wary of theodicies that explain suffering away, and holds that Scripture's deepest response is the presence of a God who entered the suffering himself.

The teaching that God governs all things, permitting what he hates and bending even real evil toward an end its author never intended, as in Joseph's words, without making the evil good or claiming we can read his purpose from inside our suffering.

The argument, associated with Alvin Plantinga, that there's no strict logical contradiction in an all-good, all-powerful God permitting evil that arises from the real freedom he gives his creatures. It shifted the debate from the logical to the evidential form of the problem.
Jesus' cry from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22:1), the sufferer's question prayed by God in human flesh.

The classical teaching that God in his divine nature isn't subject to suffering, held to protect the truth that he isn't a victim of forces greater than himself. The study notes the modern challenge to it and rests on what both sides share, that in Christ God truly entered human suffering.
Augustine's account of evil not as a thing in itself but as a corruption or absence of the good God made, the way blindness is the loss of sight rather than a substance.
The biblical prayer of complaint and protest, "How long, O LORD?", brought directly to God. Scripture models it and never rebukes it.

The storm out of which God answers Job, not with an explanation but with his presence and questions that put Job back inside a creation too large for his own accounting. The study's picture of presence over explanation.
The Christian claim that God didn't stay outside human suffering but entered it fully on a cross, so that there's no human pit he hasn't known from the inside.
The biblical hope of a renewed heaven and earth where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, and death and mourning and pain are no more. Suffering defeated rather than explained.
Christian hope grounded not in vague optimism but in the resurrection of Jesus as a claimed event in history, the assurance that suffering, real and unexplained, will finally be defeated.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: If God is good, and God is able, why does he allow suffering? It's the oldest question and the hardest, the one that drives more people from the faith than almost any other, and most studies answer it with a formula that wounds the people it means to help. This five-session study refuses the cheap answer. It takes the question at full strength, the way a thoughtful skeptic asks it, and walks toward the response Scripture finally gives: not an argument but a God who entered the suffering himself, on a cross, and walked out of the grave. It's careful with the grieving, and it never explains anyone's pain away. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are.

quoteCards: If I could reduce the suffering of the world to a paragraph that made it all make sense, that paragraph would be obscene.
The question isn't the enemy of faith. You don't cry out to a God you're sure isn't there.
Joseph called his brothers' act evil to their faces, and in the same breath said God meant it for good. He held both.
At the end of Job, God was angry not at the man who protested but at the friends who defended him with tidy theology.
God didn't give Job a reason. He gave Job himself.
The cross doesn't explain your suffering. It tells you God has been in the pit before you, as one of the crucified.
An explanation would tell you why the child died. A defeat undoes the death.
The dark is real. But the last word is a morning, and a hand on a wet face.
